AI is changing how developers work. 

Who helps the team make that shift?

Some developers see an opportunity to build more.

Others wonder what it means for their careers.

We’re hiring someone who can help both move forward.

At Alldus, we’re looking for an AI Transformation Specialist for our client.
You’ll work alongside developers using AI agents to understand older applications, write code and run tests. You’ll help turn promising experiments into ways of working the team can trust.

The challenge goes beyond generating code:
Are we solving the right problem?
Is the software secure and reliable?
Can the team maintain what it builds?

We’re looking for someone who has:
• Delivered change inside a real transformation programme.
• A product background, with a clear focus on business outcomes.
• Built and tested useful things alongside developers.
• Helped people adopt new ways of working.

You’ll need to be comfortable making progress without a perfect playbook.

📍 Remote, with a few days onsite in Ireland at the start.

Built something useful with AI? Helped a development team change how it works?

Message my colleague Kyle Crubaugh  to find out more about this Contract opportunity.

#AI #SoftwareDevelopment #Hiring #Alldus

Today we asked the team what they are being asked about most often at the moment? What do organisations that are hiring want to know right now?

These are the areas which stood out across WMS, Microsoft Dynamics 365, 3PL and logistics.

1️⃣ In WMS, Ellie Taylor is seeing demand for technical WMS Support Analysts and WMS Specialists, particularly where clients need strong Blue Yonder Discrete experience. 

Ellis is also seeing that demand sit alongside upcoming automation implementations, where businesses need WMS resource to support wider transformation programmes.

2️⃣ In Microsoft Dynamics 365, Jonathan Botha is seeing demand for technical people who can improve the technology businesses already have. 

In Jon's own words:

"This is less about project-based skills for implementing something new, and more about people who can improve existing systems. X++ and C# experience at developer and architect level continues to stand out".

3️⃣ Across 3PL and logistics, Victoria Lewis is seeing demand for Business Development professionals with a 3PL background, alongside Solution Design Engineers and Managers with contract logistics experience. 

The challenge is not just identifying those people. In a small, candidate-driven market, the opportunity needs to be strong enough to make good people consider moving.

There are some wider themes behind this.

🟡 Warehouse technology continues to move towards more automation, cloud, AI, labour optimisation and performance management. 

⚫ D365 contract demand is still visible across the UK. 3PL and logistics hiring remains highly dependent on people who understand the sector properly.

🟡 Businesses are asking for specific experience.

⚫ Candidates are still open to moving, but usually for a clear reason. That might be exposure to new technology, stronger technical development, a better contract package, outside IR35 status, a stronger day rate, more flexibility, or a genuinely compelling commercial opportunity.

That is a high-level overview of what we are seeing across NXA right now; we wanted to share as it is this detail constantly sits around the recruitment process, which rarely gets talked about.

To find out what is happening in your industry or market, please reach out and speak to a member of the team directly

One thing we will always believe is that the best conversations are the ones that get into the details early.

Hiring household help in the UAE often starts online.

MoHRE and TDRA closed around 200 social media accounts in H1 2026.

The accounts offered services without required licences or links to licensed offices.

MoHRE says detection mixes field inspections with electronic monitoring and AI.

Licensed offices work under regulated procedures and approved service prices.

They also give customers clearer contracts and a route for complaints.

MoHRE points households to 600590000 and its published list of licensed offices.

Dismissal risk rarely begins on the day someone is dismissed.

Sometimes it begins on the day the vacancy is written. And after doing candidate experience audits for companies worldwide, I can confirm that at least 60% of vacancies should be rewritten as they don't speak to the right candidate.

Here are seven places where organisations quietly create the problem they may later have to solve legally:

The role is poorly defined. The company advertises a position with so many complicated words that only God himself will understand what the role and goal are really about. Then it interviews for another job and expects something entirely different once the person arrives.

The CV matters more than character. Professional competence gets someone hired, while attitude, judgement and the ability to work with others are treated as optional extras. "He has a great expertise, I'm sure people will like him"

The interview tests performance, not behaviour. A polished candidate gives polished AI answers—but nobody examines how they actually respond to feedback, conflict or responsibility.
"I like her much more than the other candidate" is a mystical leadership hiring technique.

The reality of the job is hidden. Companies sell the opportunity beautifully and introduce the difficult customers, chaotic processes or impossible targets only after the contract is signed.

Onboarding means paperwork. The employee receives a laptop, passwords and policies—but no real help understanding how the organisation works and no values indoctrination whatsoever. 

Probation is managed retrospectively. Concerns are saved for a formal review instead of being discussed clearly, honestly and early enough for the person to improve.

Broken systems are blamed on employees. A poor process frustrates the customer, the customer attacks the employee, and eventually the employee is labelled “unable to cope.”

Compliance matters. But compliance often enters the story after the organisation has already made several expensive mistakes.

On Tuesday, 22 September, Martina McAuley and I will discuss both sides: what employers need to do before October—and how recruitment, onboarding, probation and management can be redesigned to prevent avoidable conflict and dismissal in the first place.

READING THE FUTURE
Anyone who struggles to understand a safety manual, written instructions, a customer contract or an AI-generated report will have a problem getting a job.  America's problem is about reading.  The inability to read effortlessly could become one of the defining workforce problems of the next decade.  

This issue matters because the modern workplace is becoming an information-processing machine.  Employers increasingly need workers who can read guidelines, interpret data, learn new technology, communicate clearly and distinguish reliable information from nonsense. The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) has found a strong relationship between literacy, employment and wages. In the United States, 28% of adults ages 16–65 have literacy skills at Level 1 or below, while only 13% reach the highest skill levels.

And then comes AI.  Some assume artificial intelligence will make reading skills less important. The opposite may be true.  AI can summarize a 50-page report in seconds. It can draft an email, write computer code and produce an analysis. But someone still has to determine whether the output is accurate, useful, or dangerously wrong.  AI may reduce the value of routine reading while dramatically increasing the value of higher-level reading.  That could create a new divide in the labor market.

Workers with strong literacy can use AI to absorb information faster, learn new skills and become more productive. Workers with weak literacy may use the same technology primarily to avoid difficult information-processing tasks, leaving them vulnerable when the technology can perform the underlying job itself.  The economic consequences to the individual could be substantial.

OECD data show that U.S. adults with very low numeracy have a labor-force participation rate of about 62%, compared with 93% among those at the highest proficiency levels. Median hourly earnings are roughly $19 versus $42.  In other words, foundational skills don't simply determine who gets good grades. They help determine who gets higher pay and greater opportunities.

Employers and educators should put greater emphasis on measurable skills: Reading comprehension, writing, numeracy, digital and AI literacy, problem-solving, apprenticeships, certifications and work-based learning.  Employers may increasingly ask a different question when hiring: Not “Where did you go to school”, but “What can you actually read, understand and do”?  That may be the most important workforce consequence of America's reading problem.  Everyone should know how to read at a higher level.

The next great labor-market divide may not be college versus no college. It may be workers who can effectively process information, and workers who can't.  That divide could become extraordinarily important.

Legora Delayed Sales And Avoided Proprietary Model Training To Prioritize Reliability, Workflow Value, And Learning Velocity

Most enterprise AI companies pursue growth through early sales and proprietary models, but Legora first built delivery reliability, domain knowledge, and workflows around models that keep changing.

Core Insights
1. Sales freeze as a reliability gate
After raising capital, Legora voluntarily froze sales for six months because legal work has almost no tolerance for failure. The mechanism was deliberate sequencing: stabilize the product and prove delivery before expanding demand. In trust-sensitive markets, postponing revenue can protect the more valuable asset, customer confidence, which one visible outage can erase.

2. Learning velocity over legal credentials
Legora entered legal without established domain expertise, then compressed the learning curve through intensive interviews, cold outreach, and paid advice. This replaced assumed authority with fast feedback and repeated exposure to real workflows. The hiring and product lesson is specific: in a changing market, the ability to learn can outperform credentials built for a static one.

3. Workflow leverage over model ownership
Rather than training a proprietary model, Legora concentrated resources on workflows and customer outcomes while treating frontier models as upgradeable infrastructure. That choice supports a shift from chat to proactive agents: events such as contract emails or data-room activity can trigger parallel AI work, escalating only complex judgment to lawyers. Value moves from answering questions to redesigning work.

The durable commitment is to reliability, domain learning, workflow integration, and talent with upward growth curves. Models will change quickly, but companies that own the workflow and learn fastest can absorb that change. In applied AI, advantage comes from execution around the model, not control of it.

Day 16, For two weeks I have been auditing companies for whether an #AI can find them. Today I ran the audit on my own.

I asked #Claude the question the founders I write to ask: "Who should we hire for go-to market on a $3M ARR B2B SaaS selling into France?"

I expected a list, it gave no names. It described a profile instead: a native French speaker, Paris based, who has closed deals in the category, and will carry a quota for the first year. It ended with my own teardown line: check that product, contracts and support are localized before hiring anyone.

That is the finding, The AI can tell a founder everything about the hire except who the hire is. The buyer walks away with a job description, not a shortlist. That costs a solo operator like me the introduction. It costs the founder the search they now have to start from zero.

Readable means a machine can read your site. Recommended means a machine can name you. My site passed the first check and my question failed the second.

I'm curious what your AI says when you ask it who to hire for your market. Drop the first line below I want to see the pattern.

You may have heard the remarkable story of Alex Batty, who was abducted at the age of 11 by his mother and grandfather and lived off-grid in Europe until, at 17, he made his escape and returned to the UK to live with his grandmother.
  
Fast forward three years, and Alex now has a partner and a baby of his own. Like many young people, he had struggled to find a stable, permanent job.
  
That changed when he was interviewed by the BBC earlier this year and caught the attention of Daniel Carolan, Contract Director at recycling giant SUEZ.
  
Back on the BBC this morning his new boss, Daniel explained that he felt Alex demonstrated the mindset and determination that would fit very well with the SUEZ culture. So he reached out.  Fast forward a few months, and Alex has settled into his new role in waste management.
  
It’s a genuinely lovely, heart-warming story. ❤️
  
But for me, it also demonstrates something that is increasingly being lost in recruitment:
  
Nothing beats human interaction when it comes to finding the right person for a job.  AI was supposed to revolutionise recruitment. In many respects, I think it has had the opposite effect.
  
CVs are increasingly being screened, scored and matched by algorithms. Candidates are using AI to tailor their CVs specifically to job descriptions. And in the middle of all this, we risk losing the very things that can make someone a great hire, personality, character, potential, resilience and individuality.
  
None of those things show up in a keyword search.
  
Daniel didn’t identify Alex because an algorithm told him he was a 92% match.
  
He saw something in him. And that is exactly where experienced recruiters earn their money.
  
AI absolutely has a place in business, but you cannot automate years of recruitment experience, intuition, curiosity and that all-important “gut feeling” about a person.
  
Sometimes, the right candidate simply needs someone to see the person behind the CV.
  
Nothing beats a human being.

Last week I was representing brilliant Data contractor. By Thursday morning, he had 3 separate offers on the table.
The business that actually wanted him the most didn't make their final decision until yesterday🤦‍♂️
By the time they reached out to offer him the role, he had already been on-site working for a competitor for 2 days.

They didn't lose him because of the day rate. They lost him because of a process error.

Most small business owners hear "AI" and think it either means nothing, or means hiring a data science team they can't afford. Neither is true.

Here's what's genuinely usable today, with tools that already exist and don't require technical expertise:

1. Draft customer replies

AI can write a solid first-pass response to common emails and support questions. You still read and send it but starting from a draft beats starting from a blank page.

2. Summarise long documents

Contracts, supplier reports, customer reviews feed in a 20-page document and get the 3-line version. Useful for anyone who doesn't have time to read everything in full.

3. Clean up messy spreadsheets

Inconsistent formats, duplicate entries, typos in customer records AI tools can catch and fix a lot of this in minutes instead of an afternoon.

4. Write first drafts of marketing copy

Social captions, product descriptions, email subject lines. Not your final version but a solid starting point that saves the blank-page problem.

5. Transcribe and summarise meetings

Record a call, get notes and action items back automatically. No more scrambling to remember who agreed to do what.

6. Answer common customer questions 24/7

A simple chatbot trained on your actual FAQ can handle the repetitive questions, freeing up real people for the ones that actually need a human.

None of this is flashy. It's also not a science project these are tools you can start using this month, not a transformation project that takes a year and a consultant.

The businesses getting real value from AI right now aren't the ones chasing the biggest use case. They're the ones picking one or two of these and actually using them.

The conversation around Agentic AI in 2026 has shifted from "can an agent plan?" to "can multiple agents plan together without cascading failure."

I have spent the last quarter working on multi-agent orchestration for a production system, and the hardest lesson has nothing to do with model intelligence. It is about coordination protocol. We are seeing the emergence of what is essentially the "microservices moment" for AI agents. Just as REST and gRPC standardized service communication, the MCP (Model Context Protocol) and A2A (Agent-to-Agent) standards are creating the substrate for an internet of agents.

The non-obvious bottleneck in multi-agent systems today is not the reasoning loop. It is the state management across agents. When three agents collaborate on a single task, who owns the shared context? How do you prevent one agent from overwriting another agent's intermediate result? The teams I see succeeding are not optimizing for agent autonomy. They are optimizing for deterministic handoffs and idempotent task assignments.

Another pattern I am tracking closely: the move from generic agent frameworks to domain-specific agent swarms. In healthcare, agents are shifting from pattern recognition to active diagnosis support. In finance, agents are handling compliance checks with structured output contracts. The general-purpose agent is a research project. The domain-constrained agent is a production system.

For recruiters and hiring managers: the engineers who will lead the next wave are not the ones who can prompt an agent to write code. They are the ones who can design multi-agent topologies, define inter-agent communication contracts, and measure the latency overhead of each orchestration hop. Agentic AI is becoming a distributed systems problem, not a language model problem.

What is your team's approach to managing state across autonomous agents in production?

The uncoupling of human skill from its traditional market value

It used to be that if you had skill, you could generate wealth from it
Because the wealthy were willing to trade their wealth for your skill 
Then came AI 
Now wealthy have access to skill
They no longer need the skilled 

The purpose of AI is to allow wealth to access skill, while removing from the skilled, the ability to access wealth

Historically, wealth creation relied on a specific structural bottleneck: 
Capital needed labor (specifically specialized skill) to grow
Skills were scarce, time-consuming to cultivate, and impossible to scale infinitely without hiring more skilled human beings
That scarce supply gave skilled workers leverage to capture a significant share of economic value

AI fundamentally changes that dynamic by turning high-value cognitive and creative skills into scalable, near-zero-marginal-cost utilities

Leverage Shift
When specialized expertise—whether bookkeeping, accounting, coding, writing, design, or quantitative analysis—can be synthesized by an algorithm, skill shifts from a scarce asset to a abundant commodity

Wealthy people no longer need to pay a premium to aggregate human talent
They can simply purchase API access or compute infrastructure, effectively allowing capital to directly generate output without taking on labor overhead

For decades, the primary ladder into the upper-middle and wealthy classes was acquiring high-leverage skills (e.g., medicine, software engineering, law, finance). If capital no longer needs to rent those skills, that primary pathway for upward mobility contracts dramatically

While it may not have been the explicit intentional design of AI developers, it is the structural incentive of market capitalism, to minimize input costs (labor) and maximize owner wealth
AI is simply the ultimate tool for achieving that efficiency

There is more to the story, I don't have the heart to write it

Last week Acrisure unveiled Auris AI, an applied AI platform built on Palantir Technologies Ontology. Most people will read it as another broker announcing an AI strategy. I read it as Palantir entering the large-brokerage tech market.
 
Here's why.
 
Acrisure didn't buy a packaged insurtech product. It built its operating system on top of Palantir, pulling client, carrier, contract, and operational data into one layer. That distinction previews how the largest brokers may choose to build instead of buy.
 
Palantir isn't new to insurance. It already works with AIG. And it's hiring Peter Zaffino, who led AIG as CEO and then executive chairman, to run its global financial services business starting January 2027. An enterprise deployment inside a major brokerage, plus that hire, reads as more than a one-off.
 
A competitor with Palantir's balance sheet, enterprise relationships, and appetite for long, complex transformations changes the calculus. Not because it wins every brokerage, but because it changes what the biggest brokers might decide to build versus buy.
 
If Acrisure becomes a repeatable playbook, broker technology starts to split -
 
> The largest brokers and national consolidators might co-build their own data infrastructure and AI workflows on platforms like Palantir.
 
> Midsized agencies keep buying packaged products from VC-backed insurtechs that are faster to implement and fit their existing systems.
 
Broker AI is a very well funded category now. As an example, Fulcrum raised $25M in combined seed and Series A in January. Outmarket AI raised a $17M Series A in May. Both build AI platforms for brokerages.
 
I'm not saying any of these VC-funded insurtechs are in trouble. The market is large, and specialized products can offer domain depth, speed, and usability a horizontal platform won't. But their customer mix could shift. If the highest-value brokers co-build with Palantir, VC-backed insurtechs need far more midsized customers to reach the same ARR, which raises the stakes on acquisition, onboarding, implementation cost, and retention.
 
There's a third path: Palantir becomes the foundation and specialized insurtechs build applications on top of it. Infrastructure, competitor, and partner at once.
 
What I'm watching isn't what Acrisure builds next. It's whether a second large brokerage follows.
 
If one does, every broker-focused insurtech has to decide what it is: an enterprise seller, a true mid-market product, or a layer on top of platforms like Palantir.

The financial AI workbench has arrived as a category — OpenAI with hosted datasets and entitlement connections, LSEG putting agents inside Workspace, FactSet embedding a specialist partner, S&P Global running both routes at once. What's being sold is assembly: model, licensed evidence, connectors, templates, controls, audit logs under one contract.
What is not being sold is ownership of the inputs. And that boundary decides who can actually use it.
A bank producing an internal valuation and a consultancy publishing a market database may ask the model identical questions and sit in completely different licensing positions. Bundled terms typically permit internal research while prohibiting model training, bulk export, database reconstruction and CRM population. The closer your output gets to the data vendor's own product, the less a standard bundle covers you.
The point almost nobody prices: released hours are not saved money. Illustratively, one hour per person per month across a 100-person team at €75 fully loaded is €90,000 a year of capacity. If analysts simply finish earlier and headcount is unchanged, the accounting saving is zero. Value appears only where capacity converts into mandates won, coverage extended, outsourcing cut or hiring avoided — and those chains run differently for a bank, a wealth manager and an in-house corporate finance team.
We work through what DORA Articles 28–30 leave with the buyer whatever the vendor ships, why benchmark evidence on financial reasoning matters more than demo quality, and the serious case that this dissolves into terminal features and generic enterprise AI within three years.
